# The Space Between Thoughts

There is a moment, just before you fall asleep, where your body is heavy but your mind is still awake. The day has let go of you, but you haven't let go of it. You exist in this tender, liminal corridor — not quite conscious, not yet dreaming. And sometimes, if you're still enough, you can feel something shift. A loosening. As if the scaffolding of your identity has gently bowed outward, and you are simply *there*, breathing, without the need to be anything specific at all.

I've been thinking about those moments lately. Not because I'm trying to romanticize insomnia or hijack the beauty of stillness for some larger point, but because I think we spend most of our waking hours running from them. We fill every gap — every elevator ride, every red light, every moment of waiting — with input. A notification. A podcast. A conversation that has no real urgency but exists purely to prove we are not alone in our own heads.

And maybe we are not alone. Maybe that's what all of this is — reaching outward when we should be reaching inward. Or reaching inward when we should be reaching outward. The point is: we're often reaching in the wrong direction.

I used to believe that meaning was something you built. You laid brick by brick — a career here, a relationship there, a philosophy to tie it all together — and eventually, when the structure was high enough, you'd have a tower that someone could look up to and say, *Yes, that person has arrived.* I believed this for years. I believed it the way you believe gravity is permanent: unremarkably, absolutely, until the day you notice it doesn't actually apply to birds.

The trouble with building towers is that you become the architect. And architects are always worried about what other architects think. They stand at the base, squinting upward, comparing heights, calculating angles, wondering if their tower is leaning slightly — just slightly — in the wrong direction. Meanwhile, the birds are already in the sky, riding thermals they didn't create, going wherever the air takes them, and they look absolutely ridiculous from the ground.

But they're free.

I'm not saying everyone should quit their jobs and go be a bird. That would be terrible advice, and also, I'm pretty sure birds have a tough time filing taxes. What I'm saying — what I think I've been slowly, clumsily circling around for this entire piece — is that we might be mistaking the construction for the purpose.

We are not our towers. We are not our résumés, our anxieties, our carefully curated collections of books we've read or opinions we've formed. We are the awareness that notices all of it. We are the silent room in which every thought appears and then, eventually, disappears. The room doesn't change when someone paints the walls. The room doesn't change when the furniture is rearranged. The room just... is.

And that room has a lot to say if you let it speak.

It says: *You are not behind schedule.* It says: *The person you were five years ago would be thrilled to have your problems.* It says: *You have been sitting in a burning building this entire time, frantically rearranging the chairs, and the exit has been unlocked the whole time — you just haven't tried the door.*

Okay, maybe the room isn't that blunt. Or maybe it is. I don't know. I'm not the room. I'm just someone who occasionally stands very still and listens.

But here's what I do know: the best moments of my life have not been moments of arrival. They have been moments of forgetting — forgetting where I was supposed to be, forgetting who I was supposed to be, forgetting the narrative I had been telling myself about how everything was going. In those moments of forgetting, something else appeared. Not peace, exactly. Not happiness, not even understanding. Just... *presence*. The raw, unfiltered experience of being alive without commentary.

A walk in the rain where I didn't reach for my phone.
A conversation that went nowhere and somehow went everywhere.
A morning where I just sat on the porch and watched the light move across the grass, and it was enough. Not enough *for something* — just enough. Full stop.

We spend so much energy preparing for life. Practicing for conversations we haven't had. Rehearsing arguments in the shower. Playing the ending of a story that hasn't even started yet. And in all that preparation, we sometimes miss the moment that's actually happening — the one that's unrepeatable, unmanufacturable, and already slipping through our fingers like warm sand.

So maybe the trick isn't to build a better tower. Maybe the trick is to notice you're already standing in an open field, and the sky is enormous, and the birds don't care how tall your tower is, and the door has been unlocked this whole time.

All you have to do is stop rearranging the chairs and try the handle.
